An operation is idempotent when repeating the same request has the same intended effect as making it once. A payment API can use an idempotency key to apply this rule to repeated payment requests.

For example, suppose you send a payment request with the idempotency key `order-42`. In this hypothetical API, repeating that request with the same key does not create a second charge. The API stores the result for 24 hours. During that period, you can repeat the request with `order-42` without creating another charge. After 24 hours, the stored result expires and the API treats the same key as new. You can no longer rely on the earlier request to prevent another charge.

Idempotency concerns the intended effect, so repeated requests can still produce additional log entries. It also does not guarantee authorization. Even if a request would create only one charge, idempotency alone does not tell you whether that request is authorized.
